head: 450 of 533
deck: members of Congress have a tie on the public record to Anthropic’s network: 332 through something the network or the member did, 118 only through what third parties did. The network is the company, the funders behind it, the groups they fund, and their PACs and lobbyists.
note: Third parties are lobbyists at the network’s lobbying firms, who gave their own money, and super PACs that received network money and made their own expenditures. A tie can cut either way: a statement may be criticism, and a super PAC may have spent against the member. It is not an allegation, and a contribution is not a vote.
bridge: Start with the company: its employees’ own gifts, and its PAC’s.
how: Each dot is one of the 533 members serving on Nov. 26, 2026. A tie is a public record that links the member and the network: a contribution, a lobbying report on the member’s bill, a fellow in the office, a statement. The network, by one chain: Dustin Moskovitz and Cari Tuna are the main funders of Coefficient Giving (formerly Open Philanthropy); it awarded Georgetown’s Center for Security and Emerging Technology $55.0M in 2019; that center’s witnesses have appeared before Congress 17 times.

head: At the end of 2024, 10 members now serving had received money from Anthropic’s employees or its PAC. By Sept. 30, 2026: 196.
deck: The employees gave their own money: $5.6M, 92% of it dated 2026. The company’s PAC made its first gift on record to a member now serving on June 29, 2026; by Sept. 30 it had given $200K to 81 members, 18 of whom had no gift from an employee.
note: A person’s contribution is their own money, not their employer’s. Employer is as the giver reported it to the FEC. Both counts are of the members serving on Nov. 26, 2026; the record stops at Sept. 30, 2026.
bridge: Who gave it, and who received it?
source: Source: FEC contribution records in this project’s tables: contributions to the campaign, leadership PAC or single-member joint fundraising committee of a serving member, through Sept. 30, 2026; ANTHROPAC is Anthropic PBC’s political action committee.

head: Ten givers account for 58% of the employees’ dollars. Of the ten members who received the most, six are Republicans.
deck: The filings list 89 distinct names with Anthropic as employer; half of them gave $20,500 or less. With the PAC’s gifts, Democrats received 55% of the dollars; Jon Ossoff, a Democrat, received the most.
note: Givers are not named here; two people who share a first name and a surname count as one. A total is what the committees received, not what a member asked for. Republicans are more than half of the five largest recipients, and of every longer list up to fourteen.
bridge: $5.8M in all. The large money moved another way.
how: A circle’s area is what one name as filed gave to members now serving; the smallest are drawn a little larger than scale. A member’s total counts campaign, leadership PAC and single-member joint fundraising committees.
source: Source: FEC contribution records; all years on record, through Sept. 30, 2026.

head: Anthropic announced $40.0M for Public First Action. There the trail stops: no filing in this record lists the group’s donors.
deck: What the filings do show: two super PACs the group funds, and $15.0M of independent spending for one House candidate who does not serve in Congress. This record traces no contribution to a specific expenditure.
note: The two gifts are as Anthropic announced them; the super PACs reported the spending as independent expenditures. A contribution does not direct spending.
bridge: The company’s funders gave more, and for longer.
source: Source: Anthropic’s announcements; FEC contribution and outside-spending reports of the Public First committees. Not drawn: $1.0M Public First Action passed to a third committee, and one $105K ad naming a member without saying for or against.

head: The network’s funders gave more: $170M to outside political groups since 2016, $100M of it from Dustin Moskovitz to one committee.
deck: The 26 committees with network money on record spent $541M on members now serving, from all their donors, $420M of it against Republicans. No dollar is traced from a gift to an expenditure.
note: Of the 26, 24 have gifts on record from the network; two are super PACs that Public First Action funds.
bridge: One kind of money reaches more members than any of this, and the network did not give it.
how: Each band is one giver’s money on record; a gift does not direct spending.
source: Source: FEC contribution and outside-spending reports; BEMC 4 Association’s 2022 IRS filing; Anthropic’s announcements. Not drawn: transfers between the Public First committees, and $4.3M from other individuals, not named.

head: No tie reaches more members than lobbyists’ own gifts: 326 received $1.5M from lobbyists at firms with a network client.
deck: For 302 of them a giver is named on that client’s own filings; for the other 24, only the givers’ firms are registered for it. For 83 of the 326, what third parties did is all that ties them to the network: 83 of the 118 such members among the 450 with a tie.
note: The money is the lobbyist’s own, not the client’s, and the record does not say why a gift was made. Named lobbyists only: $1.2M in 1,003 gifts.
bridge: That is the lobbyists’ own money. Anthropic’s lobbying is on another record.
how: Counted: a gift whose giver was a registered lobbyist at a firm that had a network client in that period. Each lit seat received at least one.
source: Source: lobbyists’ semi-annual contribution reports to Congress, Feb. 19, 2021 to June 30, 2026; FEC records tie each receiving committee to one member.

head: Anthropic’s reported lobbying spending is up twentyfold since 2023: $280K that year, $5.6M in the first nine months of 2026.
deck: The 2023 sum is what outside firms reported being paid to lobby for Anthropic; the 2026 sum is the lobbying expenses on the company’s own reports, January to September.
note: Amounts are as filed, rounded. A quarter with the company’s own report leaves out its outside firms’ reports. A report’s amount covers every issue on it, so 0.5% is a share of report totals, not of AI lobbying; 2025 is the last full year compared.
bridge: Small beside the field. But which bills did its reports name?
source: Source: quarterly lobbying reports (form LD-2) through Sept. 30, 2026, for Anthropic and the nine other highest-spending network clients in the years drawn; for the share, the 2019–2025 reports this project classified as naming AI or an AI bill by title, after its documented exclusions.

head: The three bills most named in lobbying reports filed for Anthropic are about chips. All six sponsors received gifts from Anthropic’s employees or its PAC.
deck: The gifts are separate campaign records: $328,500 in all. None of the specific-issue descriptions on the 68 reports states a position on a bill.
note: Naming a bill says the client lobbied on it, not which way and not whether a sponsor’s office was contacted. The gifts are individuals’ own or the PAC’s; no filing in this record ties one to a bill.
bridge: How often did a sponsor also receive a gift?
source: Source: the 68 quarterly lobbying reports filed for Anthropic, 2023 to Sept. 30, 2026 (each bill described from its official title); FEC contribution records.

head: Lobbying reports filed for Anthropic name bills by 23 members. 19 of them received gifts from Anthropic’s employees or its PAC.
deck: Among the 91 sponsors of AI bills with no bill of theirs named in a network report, it was 47; in all of Congress, 196 of 533. By chamber: 12 of the 13 senators against 60 of all 100, and 7 of the 10 House members against 136 of all 433.
note: No money is attributed to the lobbying; each gift is an individual’s own or the PAC’s. Which came first, a gift or a report, says nothing about why either was made.
bridge: The gifts and the lobbying are recent. Who was Congress hearing from before them?
how: A report that names a bill says the client lobbied on it: not which way, and not whether the sponsor’s office was contacted.
source: Source: quarterly lobbying reports filed for Anthropic (the company’s own and those of firms it hired), matched to verified sponsors (annual defence and spending bills not counted); AI bills from this project’s companion study; FEC contribution records through Sept. 30, 2026.

head: By the end of 2024, seven of the network’s funders had awarded $528M in grants, and Congress had heard from seven of their grantees.
deck: By then, ten of the members now serving had received money from Anthropic’s employees or its PAC. The grants supported work on AI, technology, biosecurity and catastrophic risk; none of the grants shown names a member of Congress as its recipient.
note: A grant to an organisation is not money to a member, and an award is not a payment on its date. Testifying is not lobbying.
source: Source: IRS Form 990 grant schedules and the funders’ own published grant lists; witness lists from congress.gov, House committee pages and Senate hearing transcripts.

head: Horizon, a network grantee, has funded 25 fellows inside Congress; 64 people went from Congress to positions with the network or its lobbying firms.
deck: Of the 64, 34 became lobbyists at firms that work for network clients. Horizon says the host manages a fellow’s work.
note: A job or a seat is not evidence about the work done in it.
bridge: Grants, hearings, fellows, jobs, money. What does that leave on file for each member?
source: Source: Horizon Institute placement pages and alumni lists, and its “Host a Fellow” page as saved in 2026; House and Senate payroll reports, lobbyists’ disclosed former posts and organisations’ staff pages; IRS Form 990 grant schedules; for the sheet, FEC contribution records through Sept. 30, 2026.

head: A record of ties, not a record of influence.
deck: The opening slide’s two members again, with what is on file for each: seven kinds of record for Ted Lieu, one for Thom Tillis.
how: Each dot is one of the 533 members serving on Nov. 26, 2026, by party; records through Sept. 30, 2026.
